207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The: Wonder Woman is DC Comics' Amazonian superheroine, created in 1941 by psychologist William Marston and famous ever since as both franchise character and feminist icon. This book asks what her seventy-five-year history of contradictions - sexy superhero and role model, mortal and goddess, American patriot and cosmopolitan - reveals about gender. Essays use Simone de Beauvoir on becoming a woman, Foucault and Butler on gender norms, and Aristotle on practical wisdom to ask whether objectified art can still show heroic virtue.
208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing: The X-Men are Marvel's team of mutant superheroes, outsiders born with powers who are feared and persecuted by the humans they protect. Since 1963 the comics have been read as an allegory for any stigmatized minority, which makes them natural philosophical ground. Essays here ask what makes someone 'normal', who Wolverine is when his memories keep failing, whether Jean Grey may sacrifice herself, and whether Magneto's violent resistance is ever justified - via Locke, Kant, Sartre, and Singer.
209 - Basketball and Philosophy - Thinki: Basketball, the fast-paced indoor sport invented in 1891 by James Naismith (himself a philosophy student), saturates American culture from Jordan and March Madness to Hoosiers. This collection treats the court as a place where big questions get played out. Essays ask how to measure greatness between Wilt and Russell, whether Hack-a-Shaq fouling is unethical, what pickup games without referees teach about justice, and what Zen masters and Aristotle have to say about the perfect jump shot.
210 - Football and Philosophy - Going De: American football, the most-watched sport in the United States, is a collision sport beloved for its strategy, pageantry, and violence. That mix makes it rich philosophical territory. Essays use Aristotle on friendship to explain teamwork, Kant and moral-luck theory to ask what fumbles and violent hits say about character, and whether a good player can be a good person. Along the way: Lombardi's obsession with winning, cheating, performance-enhancing drugs, instant replay, and whether the salary cap makes the NFL fair.
211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from: Golf is the quiet, maddeningly difficult game of hitting a small ball across vast landscapes - famously a pursuit that looks easy and proves endless. That character makes it a favorite of philosophers. Organized as eighteen 'holes', the book asks why play matters, what makes Augusta beautiful and Bobby Jones's self-imposed penalty sublime, whether golf builds moral character, how its rules expose cheating and gamesmanship, and how Confucius, Taoism, and Ben Hogan might fix your swing - or your life.
212 - The Olympics and Philosophy: The Olympic Games, reviving ancient Greece's athletic contests every four years, bill themselves as a celebration of human excellence rather than mere winning. That lofty ideal invites scrutiny. Essays weigh whether true Olympic greatness requires moral virtue, reading Aristotle's magnanimity in Eugenio Monti and Wilma Rudolph, Nietzsche's self-overcoming in Steve Prefontaine, and the Greek virtue of arete against record-obsession and cheating. Others trace competition itself from Homer's funeral games to Plato, asking what sport is ultimately for.
213 - Tennis and Philosophy - What the R: Tennis, the one-on-one racquet sport of Wimbledon and grunting baselines, is a game of split-second failure, hot tempers, and solitary excellence. This book takes its psychology and beauty seriously. David Foster Wallace argues watching Roger Federer is near-religious; other essays ask who the all-time best really is (a problem in vagueness and epistemology), why every tennis film is bad, whether McEnroe-style rage is ethical, and how the mind of a complaining player or an authoritarian parent deceives itself.
214 - The Philosophy of Ang Lee: Ang Lee is the Taiwanese-born director whose range runs from Sense and Sensibility to Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, Brokeback Mountain, and Life of Pi, often placing characters torn between tradition and desire. This book reads his career as one sustained philosophical argument about authentic selfhood. Essays use Confucian virtue and Daoist freedom to unpack Li Mu Bai and Jen, Charles Taylor and Kierkegaard on identity, and Mencius and the aesthetics of the sublime to reread Ennis and Jack's love on Brokeback Mountain.
215 - The Philosophy of the Beats: The Beats were the 1950s American counterculture writers - Jack Kerouac, Allen Ginsberg, William Burroughs, Gary Snyder - whose spontaneous prose and poetry, from On the Road to 'Howl', turned weariness with mainstream life into a wandering, drug-fueled, Zen-inflected search for meaning. This book argues they were doing philosophy as much as literature. Essays connect Kerouac's road to utopia and Mill, Burroughs's split selves to Lacan and posthumanism, Snyder to Heidegger and ecology, and Diane di Prima to French feminism.
216 - The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman: Charlie Kaufman is the American screenwriter and director of Being John Malkovich, Adaptation, Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, and Synecdoche, New York - surreal, melancholy films about memory, authorship, and selves that refuse to hold still. This book shows why he is a natural philosopher's subject. Essays read Malkovich's head-portal against Descartes and Merleau-Ponty, Eternal Sunshine against Nietzsche's eternal recurrence, Adaptation against Deleuze, and all of his films against Aristotle on friendship and Kierkegaard on despair.
